core.text: **the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense)** marks an action finished before another future action. Latin uses it in *sī* (if), *cum* (when), *postquam* (after) clauses: *cum vēnerō, gaudēbō* — when I have come (literally: will have come), I will be glad. Forms: perfect stem + *-erō, -eris, -erit, -erimus, -eritis, -erint*; passive: perfect participle + *erō, eris, erit* (*captus erit*). Latin name: *futurum exactum*.
English: *by noon he will have left*. In *if* and *when* clauses English drops it — *when you have finished, call me* — but the logic is the same: finishing first, calling second.
Perfect stem + -erō … -erint. In a sī / cum / postquam clause with a future main verb translate it as a plain present or perfect: sī vēnerit = if he comes.

invented.en: If you write the letter, I will be glad.
When we have had dinner, we will sleep.

core.text: The perfect subjunctive (the 'have done' form: *nesciō quid fēcerit*) has the same endings except *-erō* / *-erim*. The job decides: in a sī / cum / postquam clause pointing to the future it is the future perfect (*sī vēnerit, gaudēbō*); after *nē* (don't) or a question word it is the perfect subjunctive (*nē timuerīs*; *nesciō quid fēcerit*).

more.text: Also easy to confuse: the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense) ends *-ērunt* in the plural, the future perfect *-erint* — *vēnērunt* they came, *vēnerint* they will have come. The third person plural is the one place the two nearly touch.

The learner's notes: the future perfect is an action viewed as completed in the future; in English 'will have' + past participle. Latin builds the active from the 2nd stem + *-er-* + endings, with *-int* rather than *-unt* in the third plural precisely to keep it apart from the perfect; the passive is the perfect participle + *erō, eris, erit, erimus, eritis, erunt* (*captus erō*, *captī erunt*). Latin uses it freely in subordinate clauses where English has the present or perfect: *quī vīderit, crēdet* — he who has seen will believe.

Ørberg's chapter 30: *dux mīlitem laudābit, sī fortiter pugnāverit*; *discipulus laudābitur sī magistrō pāruerit et industrius fuerit*; passive *pater gaudēbit sī fīlius laudātus erit*. Irregulars follow the perfect stem: *fuerō, potuerō, voluerō, ierō*. In a main clause on its own it is rare and means a confident 'will have': *vīderimus*, we will have seen. With *cum* it stays indicative because it is a real future time, not story background (compare cum + subjunctive, Week 6).
